title: Simple Questions on the First Day of School that Teach Purpose
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart turns a routine first-day task, collecting index cards with each student's name, into an opportunity to teach purpose. Drawing on William Damon's research, he defines purpose as being driven by something larger than oneself, oriented toward a future goal or the greater good. He argues that purpose is a 'motivational fusion reactor' that answers the perennial 'When will I ever use this?' question and moves students toward ownership of their learning, yet only a small minority of students currently study with a clear sense of purpose. So on the back of the cards he asks two questions: what kind of person do you want to be, and what kind of impact do you want to have. The answers reveal far more about each child than generic prompts and introduce the idea that purpose is an inside job he will teach toward all year.
points: Stuart repurposes the first-day index card, used all year for cold-calling and seating, as a vehicle for teaching purpose.

quotes: By the end of the first day of school, I need index cards with each of my students' names on them. I'll use these to randomly call on students throughout the year during Think-Pair-Shares, doing everything in my power to ensure that every student speaks, every day, and I'll use them as a quick seating chart rearrangement tool, placing them randomly on desks for the first few weeks so that I can see how my students work in different social groupings.

Before I try explaining the purpose of my class, I want my students to take a crack at defining some purpose of their own. Granted, most of them are jacked up on nerves because it's their first day of high school, but it doesn't matter — without purpose, they'll struggle to focus all year long.
And this isn't pie in the sky stuff — it's a motivational fusion reactor. When driven by purpose, our students don't need us to repeatedly explain the answer to “When will I ever use this?
Notice how much this teaches you about a child — so much more than the “Tell me something about yourself” questions I used to have students respond to on their index cards.

But in addition to giving me some fascinating, insightful reading on the afternoon after the first day of school, these index cards have also served a much larger goal: they've introduced my students to the idea that purpose is ultimately an inside job — it will only serve to motivate them when they seek to make it central to their lives.
